paragraphs: “Do you want me to bow down to you, monk?” said Father Ferapont. “Get up!”
The monk got to his feet.
“Blessing, be blessed! Sit down next to me. Where have you come from?”

What startled the poor monk most was that Father Ferapont, for all his strict fasting and his great age, still looked like a vigorous old man. He was tall and stood perfectly straight. His face was thin, yet fresh and healthy. He plainly still had a good deal of strength, and his build was that of an athlete. He was very old, but his hair was thick and his beard full, and neither was even fully gray. Both had once been black. His eyes were large, gray and bright, though they stood out strikingly from his face. He had a broad country accent. He wore a peasant’s long reddish coat made of coarse convict cloth (as it used to be called), tied round the waist with a stout rope. His throat and chest were bare. Under the coat, his shirt of the coarsest linen was almost black with dirt, for it had not been changed in months. People said he wore thirty pounds of iron chains beneath the coat. On his bare feet were old slippers that were nearly falling apart.
“From the little Obdorsk monastery, from St. Sylvester,” the monk answered humbly. All the while his keen, curious, slightly frightened little eyes were watching the hermit.
“I’ve been to your Sylvester’s. I used to stay there. Is Sylvester well?”
The monk hesitated.
“What a senseless lot you are! How do you keep the fasts?”

“We eat according to the ancient rules of the monastery. In Lent no meals are provided on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. On Tuesday and Thursday we are given white bread, stewed fruit with honey, wild berries or salted cabbage, and porridge of coarse meal. On Saturday there is white cabbage soup, noodles with peas, and kasha, all of it made with hemp oil. On weekdays we get dried fish and kasha along with the cabbage soup. In Holy Week, from Monday to Saturday evening, six whole days, nothing at all is cooked. We have only bread and water, and little of that, and if possible we do not eat every day, as is ordered for the first week of Lent. On Good Friday we eat nothing. On the Saturday, too, we must fast until three o’clock, and then we take a little bread and water and drink one cup of wine. On Holy Thursday we drink wine and have something cooked without oil, or nothing cooked at all, because the council of Laodicea says of Holy Thursday: ‘It is unseemly to relax the fast on Holy Thursday and so dishonor the whole of Lent!’ That is how we keep the fast. But what is that beside you, holy Father,” added the monk, growing more confident, “who take nothing but bread and water all year round, even at Easter? What we eat in two days lasts you a full seven. Your great abstinence is truly marvelous.”
“And mushrooms?” Father Ferapont asked suddenly.
“Mushrooms?” the monk repeated, taken aback.

“Yes. I can do without their bread. I don’t need it at all. I can go off into the forest and live on mushrooms or berries. But they can’t do without their bread here, and that’s why they’re in bondage to the devil. These days the unclean say there’s no need for such fasting. Proud and unclean is their judgment.”
“Och, true,” sighed the monk.
“And have you seen devils among them?” Ferapont asked.
“Among them? Among whom?” the monk asked timidly.

“Last year on Trinity Sunday I went to see the Father Superior, and I haven’t been back since. I saw a devil sitting on one man’s chest, hiding under his cassock, only his horns sticking out. Another had one peeping out of his pocket, with sharp eyes, and it was afraid of me. Another had settled in somebody’s unclean belly. Another was hanging round a man’s neck, and the man was carrying him about without seeing him.”
“You—you can see spirits?” the monk asked.

“I tell you, I can see. I see right through them. When I came out from the Superior’s, I saw one hiding from me behind the door. A big one, a yard and a half high or more, with a thick long gray tail. The tip of the tail was in the crack of the door, and I was quick. I slammed the door and pinched his tail in it. He squealed and began to struggle. I made the sign of the cross over him three times, and he died on the spot, like a crushed spider. He must be rotting there in the corner and stinking by now, but they don’t see it, they don’t smell it. It’s a year since I was there. I’m telling you this because you’re a stranger.”

“Your words are terrible! But, holy and blessed Father,” said the monk, who was getting bolder and bolder, “is it true what people say about you, even in far-off lands, that you are in constant communication with the Holy Ghost?”
“He does fly down sometimes.”
“How does he fly down? In what form?”
“As a bird.”
“The Holy Ghost as a dove?”
“There’s the Holy Ghost, and there’s the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit can appear as other birds. Sometimes as a swallow, sometimes as a goldfinch, sometimes as a blue-tit.”
“How can you tell him from an ordinary tit?”
“He talks.”
“How does he talk? In what language?”
“Human language.”
“And what does he say to you?”
“Why, today he told me a fool would come to see me and ask me improper questions. You want to know too much, monk.”
“Your words are terrible, most holy and blessed Father,” the monk said, shaking his head. Yet there was doubt in his frightened little eyes.
“See this tree?” Father Ferapont asked, after a pause.
“I see it, blessed Father.”
“You think it’s an elm. To me it’s a different shape.”
“What shape?” asked the monk, after waiting in vain for him to go on.
“It happens at night. Do you see those two branches? At night it is Christ stretching out His arms to me, searching for me with those arms. I see it plainly, and I tremble. It’s terrible, terrible!”
“What’s terrible about it, if it is Christ Himself?”
“Why, He’ll seize me and carry me off.”
“Alive?”
“In the spirit and glory of Elijah, haven’t you heard? He’ll take me up in His arms and carry me away.”

The monk went back to the cell he was sharing with one of the brothers, and he was greatly perplexed. Even so, in his heart he revered Father Ferapont more than Father Zossima. He was all in favor of fasting, so it did not seem strange to him that a man who kept such a rigid fast as Father Ferapont should “see marvels.” His words certainly sounded queer, but only God could say what lay hidden in them. And were worse words and deeds not commonly seen in people who have given up their minds for the glory of God? The tale of the devil’s tail caught in the door he was ready and eager to believe, and not only as a figure of speech. Besides, before coming to the monastery he had been strongly prejudiced against the institution of “elders.” He knew it only from hearsay and thought it a harmful novelty. He had not been at the monastery long before he noticed the secret grumbling of some shallow brothers who disliked it. He was, besides, a meddlesome, curious man who poked his nose into everything. That was why the news of the fresh “miracle” performed by Father Zossima left him so deeply perplexed. Alyosha remembered afterwards how their inquisitive guest from Obdorsk kept flitting from one group to another, listening and asking questions among the monks crowded inside and outside the elder’s cell. At the time, though, he paid him little attention, and only recalled it later.

In fact, he had no thought to spare for it. Father Zossima had grown tired again and gone back to bed. As he was closing his eyes, he thought of Alyosha and sent for him. Alyosha ran to him at once. No one else was in the cell except Father Païssy, Father Iosif and the novice Porfiry. The elder opened his weary eyes, looked hard at Alyosha, and suddenly asked him:
“Are your people expecting you, my son?”
Alyosha hesitated.
“Do they not need you? Did you not promise someone yesterday that you would visit them today?”
“I did promise—my father—my brothers—others too.”

“You see, you must go. Do not grieve. Be sure that I will not die without your being here to hear my last word. I will say that word to you, my son. It will be my last gift to you. To you, dear son, because you love me. But now go and keep your promise.”

Alyosha obeyed at once, though it was hard to leave. But the promise that he would hear the elder’s last word on earth, and that it would be his own last gift to him, filled Alyosha’s soul with a thrill of rapture. He hurried so that he could finish what he had to do in the town and come back quickly. Father Païssy, as they left the cell together, also spoke some words of exhortation that moved and greatly surprised him.

“Remember always, young man,” Father Païssy began, without any preface, “that the science of this world has grown into a great power. In the last century especially, it has analyzed everything divine that has come down to us in the holy books. After that cruel analysis, the learned men of this world have nothing left of all that was once sacred. But they have analyzed only the parts and missed the whole, and their blindness is truly marvelous. The whole still stands firm before their eyes, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Has it not lasted nineteen centuries? Is it not still a living, moving power in the soul of the individual and in the masses of the people? It is just as strong and alive even in the souls of atheists, who have destroyed everything! Even those who have renounced Christianity and attack it still follow the Christian ideal in their inmost being. Until now neither their cleverness nor the ardor of their hearts has been able to create a higher ideal of man and of virtue than the one Christ gave long ago. When they have tried, the result has been only grotesque. Remember this above all, young man, because your dying elder is sending you out into the world. Perhaps, when you remember this great day, you will not forget my words. They come from my heart, for your guidance, since you are young, and the temptations of the world are great, beyond your strength to bear. Well, now go, my orphan.”

With these words Father Païssy blessed him. As Alyosha left the monastery and turned them over in his mind, he suddenly saw that he had found a new and unexpected friend, a warmly loving teacher, in this austere monk who until now had been stern with him. It was as if Father Zossima had left him to Father Païssy at his death. “Perhaps that is exactly what passed between them,” Alyosha thought suddenly. The philosophical reflections he had just heard so unexpectedly showed how warm Father Païssy’s heart was. He was in a hurry to arm the boy’s mind for the struggle with temptation, and to protect the young soul left in his care with the strongest defense he could think of.
